title: Kierkegaard’s Knight of Faith — commitment beyond easy certainty
when: Kierkegaard developed these themes in Copenhagen in the early 1840s. Fear and Trembling appeared in 1843 under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio; its narrator should not automatically be treated as Kierkegaard speaking directly.
people: Søren Kierkegaard; Johannes de Silentio, the pseudonymous narrator; Abraham and Isaac, figures in the biblical story.
origin: Nineteenth-century Danish Lutheran culture and debates about Hegelian system-building; the book is a literary-philosophical meditation on Genesis 22, Abraham’s binding of Isaac.
idea: De Silentio contrasts infinite resignation—relinquishing what one loves—with Abraham’s faith, which he portrays as somehow receiving finite life back while remaining devoted to God. From the standpoint of universal ethics, Abraham’s intended sacrifice cannot be explained as an ordinary moral duty; the narrator calls this the paradox of faith and emphasizes its anguish and isolation. This is not a simple license to break moral rules. Nor does the phrase “leap of faith” occur in Kierkegaard’s writings: it is a later shorthand for broader discussions of qualitative change and religious commitment.
relevance: The book still presses a hard question: when someone claims private conviction overrides a shared moral rule, what could distinguish profound commitment from self-deception or danger? Kierkegaard’s uncertain narrator keeps the case unsettling rather than offering an easy recipe. That tension matters in debates about conscience, religious belief, and the limits of ethical explanation.
